scenes.visual: Portrait pushes in slowly; name and dates appear.

scenes.tts: The most durable metaphor in enzymology escaped almost by accident. Closing an 1894 lecture, Fischer reached for an image to explain why an enzyme would tear one sugar apart and ignore its near-twin: enzyme and substrate had to fit "like lock and key." He distrusted it the moment he said it.

scenes.tts: By 1898 he was publicly walking it back, insisting the specificity lay in "the asymmetric structure of the enzyme molecule" and that he had used the picture only to make the thought clearer.

scenes.tts: Then the warning this chapter proves him right to give: the idea "can only be thoroughly tested when we are able to isolate the enzymes in a pure state and thus investigate their configuration." It took most of a century.
scenes.visual: warning; pure enzyme isolated; most of a century

scenes.tts: When crystallographers finally held a pure enzyme and looked, the brass lock turned out to flex — closing around its substrate, and gripping the fleeting transition state tighter still. That correction is what Koshland named induced fit.
scenes.visual: crystallographers; flexing jaws; transition state; induced fit
scenes.narration: When crystallographers finally held a pure enzyme and looked, the brass lock turned out to flex — closing around its substrate, and gripping the fleeting transition state tighter still. That correction is what Koshland named induced fit.

scenes.tts: Fischer reached the lock-and-key idea the way he read structure off behavior everywhere else: he built sugars from glycerol to prove life held no chemistry beyond the ordinary, declaring that science had stripped the "lifeforce" of "this last hiding-place." The phenylhydrazine that fingerprinted those sugars also, slowly, poisoned him; in 1919, dying of an inoperable cancer, he took his own life.
